title: What Comes Next: A Queue That Gives the Earliest First, Ties in Order, and a Window That Drops From the Front

questions.question: A std::priority_queue<int> is given 5, 1, 9 and 3. What does top() return?
options: 9: it is a max-heap, so the greatest comes first
questions.explanation: A schedule wants the earliest, so it must compare the other way round.

questions.question: Eight events are scheduled at the same time. A priority_queue compares only the time. In what order do they come out?
options: An order the standard does not promise, which was 0 2 6 5 7 4 1 3 on libstdc++
questions.explanation: Each event gets a sequence number, compared after the time.

questions.question: What makes the event queue give ties in the order they were scheduled?
options: A sequence number given at scheduling and compared after the time
questions.explanation: Ten thousand events over 500 times came out sorted with ties in order.

questions.question: A window of 1000 is kept over 5000 readings by erasing the front of a vector. How many elements are moved, and by pop_front on a deque?
questions.explanation: A vector is contiguous: removing the first moves all the rest.

questions.question: Why does Window keep a running sum?
options: To be faster than a deque
Adding the new reading and removing the one that left costs one step, where a pass over the window for every reading costs as much as the erase
The mean must be an integer
questions.explanation: After a thousand readings of 7.0 the mean was within 1e-9 of 7.

questions.question: Why can you not cancel an event once it is in the queue?
options: A priority queue only gives its top, so a simulation marks an event cancelled and skips it when it comes out
questions.explanation: That is a limit of the container, stated in the lesson.
